questions.q: Why is general-purpose `new`/`delete` a poor fit for a market-data processor allocating one small object per tick thousands of times a second?
options: Its generality (handling any size, tracking variable-size free blocks, often synchronizing shared state) makes individual allocation cost unpredictable, creating exactly the kind of tail-latency risk a low-latency system needs to avoid
new and delete are incapable of allocating small objects
new and delete only work in single-threaded programs
There is no real performance difference between general-purpose and custom allocators
questions.explain: General-purpose allocators trade predictability for flexibility -- a given new call's cost can vary noticeably depending on internal allocator state, which is a real problem for latency-sensitive, high-frequency allocation.

questions.q: How does an arena (bump) allocator satisfy an allocation request?
options: By advancing a pointer within one large pre-allocated block -- no searching or per-allocation bookkeeping required
By calling the operating system for new memory on every single allocation
By searching a list of free blocks of varying sizes to find the best fit
By asking the garbage collector to find available memory
questions.explain: Arena allocation is just pointer arithmetic -- about as fast as an allocator can be, at the cost of having no way to free an individual object.

questions.q: What is the real limitation of an arena allocator that makes it unsuitable for objects with unpredictable, individually varying lifetimes?
options: It has no way to free an individual object -- memory can only be reclaimed all at once via reset()
It can only allocate objects smaller than 8 bytes
It requires a garbage collector to function
It is slower than general-purpose new for every allocation
questions.explain: An arena's only reclamation mechanism is resetting the whole block at once -- fine for batch-lifetime objects, but wrong for objects (like individual Orders) that come and go unpredictably.

questions.q: How does a pool allocator support individual allocate/deallocate calls, unlike an arena?
options: It pre-allocates fixed-size slots and threads a free list through unused ones, so deallocating a slot just pushes it back onto the free list for reuse
It calls the operating system to free memory on every deallocate() call
It is identical to an arena allocator in every respect
It uses a different-sized block for every single allocation request
questions.explain: A pool's free list of fixed-size slots is what enables cheap individual allocate/deallocate -- deallocating just pushes the slot back onto the list rather than reclaiming the whole block.

questions.q: What is the specific job of placement new, as distinct from an allocator's allocate() call?
options: It constructs an object (runs its constructor) at a specific, already-allocated memory address, rather than also allocating memory for it
It allocates memory but never runs a constructor
It is a synonym for calling delete on an object
It automatically chooses the best allocator for a given object type
questions.explain: Placement new separates 'get memory' (the allocator's job) from 'construct a valid object in that memory' (placement new's job) -- a distinction ordinary new T(...) hides by doing both at once.
